title: Which one dissolves in oil?
hook: Salt and sugar vanish in water. Shake them with an oily liquid and see what happens.

knows: that salt and sugar dissolve in water
that oil and water do not mix
doesNotKnow: that water molecules have charged ends and oily molecules do not
that a liquid dissolves what it attracts about as strongly as it attracts itself

misconception: If something dissolves in water it dissolves in anything; 'oil and water don't mix' is just a rule.
objective: The learner can explain that iodine (no charged ends) dissolves in hexane while salt (ions) and sugar (charged ends) stay as grains, because each liquid dissolves what attracts it the way its own molecules do: like dissolves like.

claims.text: Hexane is an oily liquid found in petrol, and its molecules have no charged ends (it is nonpolar).
claims.source: n-Hexane is a C6 alkane, a component of gasoline (petrol) and a common nonpolar solvent; dipole moment about 0 D (CRC Handbook, 'Dipole moments').

claims.text: Water molecules have charged ends (water is polar).
claims.source: Water dipole moment 1.85 D (CRC Handbook, 'Dipole moments'); partial charges on O and H (Atkins & Jones, Chemical Principles, ch. on intermolecular forces).

claims.text: Salt (sodium chloride, made of + and − ions) and sugar (sucrose, whose molecules have charged ends) dissolve well in water but practically not at all in hexane.
claims.source: CRC Handbook, 'Physical constants of organic/inorganic compounds': NaCl 36 g/100 g water, insoluble in nonpolar solvents; sucrose about 200 g/100 g water, insoluble in hexane (O–H groups make it polar).

claims.text: Iodine has no charged ends; it dissolves in hexane, giving a violet solution, and dissolves only slightly in water (pale brown).
claims.source: I2 is a nonpolar diatomic molecule. Solubility in water about 0.3 g/L at 25 °C (CRC Handbook); violet solutions in alkanes such as hexane (Greenwood & Earnshaw, Chemistry of the Elements, ch. 17).

claims.text: A liquid dissolves what pulls on it about as strongly as its own molecules pull on each other: like dissolves like.
claims.source: 'Like dissolves like' rule of thumb for polar/nonpolar solubility (Atkins & Jones, Chemical Principles, ch. on solutions). It is a rule of thumb, not a law; the stage dots and grains are a cartoon, not counts.

claims.text: (Recall) Grease does not dissolve in water but does in a nonpolar solvent such as white spirit.
claims.source: White spirit is a mixture of C7–C12 aliphatic and alicyclic hydrocarbons (WHO IPCS Environmental Health Criteria 187), used to dissolve oils and greases; fats and greases are largely nonpolar.

recall.question: A grease stain will not wash out with water. Which is most likely to dissolve it?
options: an oily, nonpolar solvent such as white spirit
recall.why: Grease has no charged ends, so it mixes with liquids that also have none. Like dissolves like.
